text:
If the Love Isn’t Coming Yet
If you weren’t loved well as a child, “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn’t close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.
Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. It’s scaffolding, and it isn’t a test of whether you were loved enough.
Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. What people most often say helped is letting their defenses down. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard (see the section Hear the Guard First).
If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. That takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.
Your little one might not take it well at first. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!” Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow.

text:
Forgiveness without bypass
We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. But if we stay in the anger forever, we let the injury dictate how we live our lives in the present. Holding all of this just means remembering that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it. We have to keep our boundary with them, especially after forgiveness, which can weaken it. One day we may find that we have forgiven them for not knowing better, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
You might say to the part of you that got hurt, “I’m not going to use spiritual mumbo jumbo to shush your cries and make you forgive before you're ready. But I’m also not going to build our whole life around this wound forever.”
Forgiving yourself
For self-forgiveness, name what you regret doing, and take responsibility for just that part. Let yourself feel the remorse by taking in the harm done, and see how it went against your values. Just stop short of making yourself a permanent criminal by identifying with the behaviors you're now abandoning.
Do what you can to put it right. Every so often, come back to how you got to be someone who could do that, until you understand the pattern well enough that it can't drive you anymore.

Once you’ve got your bearings, make your first wish.
"Please show me the next truth. The next symbol or feeling. The question or action that's useful for me at this time, and no more than I can handle."
Stay awake when your mind likes to escape
If your mind keeps drifting off, sit up and open your eyes. Then feel your feet on the floor, and just let your breathing go at its own pace. Tell yourself, "I'm not going anywhere. I'm happily arriving more fully here each moment."
Pick something in the room to look at, and feel your spine at the same time (focusing on two things makes it harder for the mind to use multitasking mode to wander). Then ask yourself what the daydreaming is doing for you. Is it bringing you guidance? Does it help you work through a feeling, or are you using it to avoid something?

text:
Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
Set one boundary. “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Handle that task you’ve been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! Maybe your little one had grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, and maybe you’ve done it too, so this is how they start to believe you.
You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. “What’s an ‘internal attack’?” Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them, and if they’re sarcastic about it, you hear it out instead of snapping back (they don’t trust you yet, and you don’t ask them to). If they complain about something and they’re right, you say so. All of that shows them, as clearly as the clean room did, that you’re safe to be around and that you accept them. Love needs both, but without warmth they can still feel like they’re only being put up with.
Plenty of people are still at the putting-up-with part. Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector’s plain acts, and the warmth can come after. That feels backwards, since you’d think you have to feel it first before you could do anything for them. But yeah, bonding starts somewhere. And this is not to say you’ve never done anything to care for yourself. If not, you’d be dead right now. But now we’re doing more of it on purpose, as a base for love to grow.

text:
Borrow Hindsight
I sometimes ask: “How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?” It’s a question borrowed from your future self, and I wouldn’t take their answer as gospel. I don’t think a perfect Higher Self is waiting in there with the answers, either (more on that in How This Relates to IFS).
That future you also knows why you can’t pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they’d just make you some food. If you can’t picture them, make the food yourself, and don’t bother faking a feeling first. A “no” or a pause can count as the food, too.
You can also borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, as long as you don’t assume they’ll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

text:
The Parent You Inherited
I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. Five Stages of Reparenting

2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby doll etc.
3. Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them.
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. text:
If the Love Isn’t Coming Yet
If you weren’t loved well as a child, “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn’t close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.
Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. It’s scaffolding, and it isn’t a test of whether you were loved enough.
Once you take the hostility out, there’s room for warmth. What people most often say helped is letting their defenses down. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard (see the section Hear the Guard First).
If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. Trust takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.
Your little one might not take it well at first. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!” Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow.

We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. But if we stay in the anger forever, we let the injury dictate how we live our lives in the present. So how do we hold all of this? We just remember that it can all be true at once. text:
The Parent You Inherited
I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide whatever part of their real self wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.
If it’s a critic, the parent you inherited also measures whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, and then attacks you from both sides: you’re not good enough, and anything that does look good is fake anyway. That second one means nothing you do could ever count, and it’s one place feeling fake can come from. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying “Trust me,” of course your little one doesn’t answer.
But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.
A good routine still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s run in the warden’s tone. Talking back to the warden can feel disloyal, so I’d give that voice a name of its own, like the Critic. Then start a little rap sheet of its lines, with who used to say them and when (ST-CA has this as an exercise, section 18.12.2). Comfort your little one before you answer any of it. Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.
The voice can also pile on. You feel sad, then call yourself pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide. You could probably have handled the sadness on its own. The name-calling, though, is where your Nurturer can step in.

text:
Five Stages of Reparenting
For now, I think of the whole path in five fairly predictable stages. You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):
1. You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting.
2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby doll etc.
3. Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
4. Adult mode itself — after enough practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them.
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!
Whichever stage you’re at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life. Your little one starts believing the grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you’re wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore.
Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, after all. Say your boss asks you to stay late again. You tell them no and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen.

text:
Pattern 10: Meta Model questions — the de-hypnosis tool
To 'Milton Model' is to open things up, so the listener can fill in what fits for them. To 'Meta Model' is to stop and ask, "What do you mean by that?" In order to be ethical with people, you need to do both.
When something sounds true but vague, ask, "What do you mean, specifically?" Then, "According to who? Compared to what?" If you hear "always" or "never," check whether it's really every time. If someone's afraid of doing something, ask what exactly would happen if they did. And ask how they know, and what evidence would change their mind.
So when someone is starting to tense up in their body, use the Milton Model to help them soften, and reach for the Meta Model when you feel you're losing track of what's really going on.

text:
Differentiation can happen right inside a family, religion, community or relationship. You’d still belong, just selectively. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that’s your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who’ve been absorbed into each other.
Day to day, differentiation looks something like this:
- Caring about somebody’s feelings without automatically adopting their opinions or sacrificing your own ground. Their reasons can still change your mind, though.
- Noticing when you agreed in the moment and disagree later: “Wait, why was I nodding along?”
- Noticing when what you thought you knew suddenly feels like water dripping through your hand because of praise or pity, fear or attraction, or something that really resonates with you.
- Disappointing people and withstanding social pressure, and still being recognizably yourself wherever you are (maybe louder in some places). That one can take a while.
- Questioning what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort, and without having to stop loving anyone over it.
Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. Sometimes you need to take a break from a family, group or relationship, even if they aren’t doing anything to you. Simply being around them may pull you into that programmed space where listening to what you really want becomes harder. Some people come back later on different terms, and sometimes the break has to be long-term because the pattern of losing yourself with them is deeply entrenched. As you differentiate, you learn to tell which of those apply.
Key developed this identity and differentiation portion of the method, drawing on Murray Bowen’s family-systems work and her own self-therapy.

text:
The 15-minute daily practice
You don't need to learn a second script for this. It's the same process (gather your attention, notice what's here, respond, wait, and come all the way back), just for fifteen minutes or so. That is long enough to induce yourself (it only takes a few minutes), practice and let it unfold at its own pace, and come out again (that takes a few minutes too). Fifteen minutes is just a handy appointment with yourself, though, and your feelings don't have to keep to it. Five minutes is plenty to see what happens when you simply sit in silence, listening, and you can interrupt yourself at any time to change direction if that feels better.
You can also try other ways of inducing yourself, such as becoming aware of 3 things you can see, 3 things you can hear, 3 things you can feel in your body; then 2 of each, 1 of each. Then count from 5 to 1 and begin to listen. Choose one way to induce yourself. You don't need to try all of them (in fact, stacking them might be counter-productive).
Once you have practiced listening a few times with the recordings, you may want to shorten them to speed up your induction, or even practice without playing them back at all. On the other hand, if you like using the recordings, there is no reason to stop. (Once you know the induction well, the cue from "A shortcut back into hypnosis" can shorten it too.)
As you come out of the process, ask yourself what needed warmth, and what needed to be protected. What do you need to do differently to be more in accord with truth and love and life? Is there something you want to explore more fully or a capacity you want to build? And most importantly, what can you now carry yourself that you used to have to borrow? If you identified something you needed to do differently, make a plan with yourself to do that thing. The more specific you can be, the more likely you are to change: “If _________ (fill in the cue for the old pattern), then I will do ________ (fill in a small action that will begin to change the pattern).” Then check back later and see how you are doing – sleeping, relating, functioning, etc., not only how impressive the session felt.
